lede.text: The central dispute is whether First Nations policy should primarily secure recognition, self determination and a voice in governing decisions, or be judged by equal practical outcomes and universal citizenship. Supporters frame Victoria’s Statewide Treaty Bill 2025 as practical self determination, establishing Gellung Warl to represent First Peoples and build on Yoorrook’s truth telling work. Opponents, including Melina Bath’s Liberals and Nationals, argue the bill separates Victorians, lacks accountability and would commit escalating public funding from $24 million to more than $70 million, while Greens criticise Labor’s incomplete implementation. The terms have shifted from federal constitutional recognition and the Voice toward state treaty and truth telling, with Victoria’s first treaty framed as a longer project of self determination rather than a single referendum.

sections.question: What policy changes, government announcements and implementation evidence concern First Nations across the public record since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Since July 2024, the public record shows several policy changes and announcements concerning First Nations. The Commonwealth released its Closing the Gap 2024 annual report and 2025 implementation plan, which the government says outlines actions taken over the past year and its strategy for the year ahead, focusing on "creating jobs and economic empowerment for remote communities, easing housing overcrowding and improving safety" and "easing cost-of-living pressures and improving food security in remote communities". The Australian Government also committed "$70 million for implementation of the First Nations Clean Energy Strategy 2024-2030 (the Strategy) over three years from 2025-26", which includes objectives for assisting First Nations project ownership and equity stakes. A revised Indigenous Procurement Policy was released in July, and the National Indigenous Australians Agency was asked whether it had provided advice to departments on applying it to identify First Nations-led businesses. The government also noted the First Nations Health Worker Traineeship Program, which commenced in July 2023, has seen "more than 550 enrolments" and "152 trainees have already completed their studies".

In Victoria, the Allan Labor government introduced and debated the Inquiries Amendment (Yoorrook Justice Commission Records and Other Matters) Bill 2024, which would allow the Yoorrook Justice Commission to make closure or restriction orders over certain First Peoples' records for 99 years. Government speakers said this enshrines Indigenous data sovereignty principles and was requested by the commission. The opposition (Liberals and Nationals) opposed the bill, with government speakers accusing them of "backflipping on their support for Victoria's treaty" and "walking out on Aboriginal Victorians". Greens speakers supported the bill but criticised the government for accepting "less than 15 per cent" of the Yoorrook Justice Commission's recommendations, saying dozens remain unimplemented, including on child protection, the minimum age of criminal responsibility and bail.

In federal parliament, opposition senators criticised the government's Closing the Gap approach. One senator claimed the Prime Minister "continues to refuse coalition calls for an audit" and that in central Australia he "tried to sell an existing funding stream for remote communities as if the $842 million was new money", when much of it was a continuation of the Northern Territory Remote Aboriginal Investment agreement. The same senator also said there "remain several targets with no data" on family violence. A government senator responded that the government is "proud to be delivering practical programs" and highlighted the traineeship program's results.

sections.question: What do bills, government releases, contracts, grants and disclosure records reveal about First Nations, and what remains unproven since July 2024?
sections.answer:
The parliamentary record since July 2024 shows several Senate divisions on First Nations matters, but no bill or motion succeeded in changing policy. On 25 June 2026, a motion by Senator Nampijinpa Price (at the request of Senator Wendy Askew) to force the Minister for Indigenous Australians to table correspondence and records since 2 July 2024 was defeated 24–32. On 10 September 2024, a Coalition-led motion to establish a Select Committee on First Nations Representative Bodies, co-sponsored by Senators Lambie and Thorpe, failed on a 32–32 tie. On 22 August 2024, a Greens motion on Missing and Murdered First Nations Women and Children was first blocked 12–24, then a procedural question passed 22–12, but the record does not show the substantive motion succeeding. On 26 November 2024, Senator Lidia Thorpe’s amendment to the Wage Justice for Early Childhood Education and Care Workers Bill, which noted more than 22,900 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in out-of-home care, was defeated 12–33. On 4 July 2024, the Senate did refer the Truth and Justice Commission Bill 2024 to the Joint Standing Committee on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs for inquiry and report by 11 February 2025, carried 32–26.

Government releases and grants show funding commitments and consultation plans, but not delivery or payment. The NSW Minister for Aboriginal Affairs and Treaty, David Harris, announced 2024 NAIDOC Grants recipients as at 7 July 2024, noting AANSW was “still confirming funding agreements with a small number of recipients.” The 2024/2025 Sound NSW grants include “two new funds specifically designed to boost First Nations artists.” A NSW campaign against coercive control, launched in June 2024 and expanded via NITV, was independently found to have increased understanding from “1 in 3 people pre-campaign to 1 in 2 post-campaign.” A federal statement claims “record funding in health, education, housing including a $299 million investment to double our successful Remote Jobs program,” and a NSW reform agreement gives child protection caseworkers a 4 per cent pay rise backdated to 1 July 2024 plus 0.5 per cent superannuation. The Prime Minister, in remarks on the failed Voice referendum, said “First Nations people themselves were determined, they wanted it put to a vote,” and took responsibility for the decision.

What remains unproven is substantial. The record contains no evidence that any announced grant, fund, or pay increase was actually paid or delivered, only that recipients were being confirmed, funds were “designed,” and contracts “went live from 1 July 2024” for a NSW maintenance hub. The $30 million surgery injection and $200 million investment since 2024 are repeated claims without proof of expenditure. The 2026 program “will expand” First Nations artists, but no artists or payments are listed. A review consulting “Aboriginal-led organisations” is due to report in the second half of 2025, with no outcome recorded. No passage proves political influence from any connection, and no passage establishes that any First Nations policy goal—such as the Truth and Justice Commission inquiry’s report—was achieved.

sections.question: What have MPs said about reconciliation and recognition of First Nations peoples since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several Victorian Labor MPs spoke in support of the Inquiries Amendment (Yoorrook Justice Commission Records and Other Matters) Bill 2024, framing it as part of a broader commitment to reconciliation and truth-telling. One MP said the bill was "actually bringing together our community" and "closing the gap by listening to our First Nations people," while criticising the opposition for objecting to it. Another Victorian Labor MP expressed pride "in being part of a Victorian Labor government that is leading the nation when it comes to progressing the aspirations of the Uluru Statement from the Heart through voice, treaty and truth," and criticised the Victorian Liberal-Nationals for opposing the bill, linking their stance to figures like John Howard and Peter Dutton. A third MP, who described being "called to Yoorrook," said the government's approach builds "on our commitment to truth-telling, because unless you have a record of the truth you cannot move forward."

In the same Victorian debate, Greens MP Ellen Sandell said her party would support the bill, which "will entrench principles of Indigenous data sovereignty within Victorian law," but criticised the Labor government for accepting "less than 15 per cent" of the Yoorrook Justice Commission's recommendations and rejecting others outright, including on the minimum age of criminal responsibility and bail. She said First Peoples are "sick and tired of telling governments the solutions that they need in their communities and then having those solutions completely ignored." A separate Victorian motion noted that Reconciliation Week 2026 would have the theme "All In," which "calls on Australians to actively commit to reconciliation, recognising it as a shared responsibility rather than one that rests solely with First Nations peoples."

At the federal level, a government response to a question stated that the government is "determined and optimistic about closing the gap for First Nations people" and is "building on what works: listening to First Nations people, partnering with their organisations and investing in community led solutions." The Prime Minister, reflecting on the 2023 Voice referendum, said he took responsibility for the decision to hold it, noting it was "the first and only referendum that's been held this century," and that "history will continue to move forward, but it doesn't move forward in a straight line." A government senator also said the government "is resolutely committed to reconciliation and celebrating the profound contribution that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples make to our nation," and noted that all health ministers had endorsed the release of a report on First Nations health care in prisons in December 2024.

sections.question: What was said in parliament about the Voice to Parliament referendum since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Since July 2024, several speakers have addressed the 2023 Voice to Parliament referendum. A government senator, responding to a question about truth-telling and treaties, said the Prime Minister spoke at the stolen generations breakfast and, while the referendum "was not the result that we wanted and that has caused harm to many in the community," he "doesn't regret wanting to enlarge our nation." The senator added that the government respects the result but "will always listen to First Nations people."

A senator from the crossbench described the referendum's failure as "devastating" and "a huge setback for our Indigenous brothers and sisters," arguing the government "must lead" with a "strong, ambitious agenda on Indigenous policy." Another senator claimed the coalition campaigned on "'vote no and get nothing', and that's exactly what they delivered," while a government senator said the Prime Minister's 2022 election-night commitment to a referendum "set an aspiration for so many Australians."

In contrast, a coalition senator said the verdict was "blunt, unambiguous and secured in a democratic process," noting 61 per cent of Australians voted no. A One Nation senator in the Victorian Parliament called the referendum "racist and divisive," citing strong "no" votes in her electorate, and criticised the Premier for continuing treaty negotiations. Another One Nation senator criticised South Australia's Premier for legislating an Aboriginal voice to parliament "despite South Australia voting against it in the Voice referendum." A coalition senator also rejected the idea that voting no "somehow mean[s] Australia is a racist country."

sections.question: How has parliament discussed Closing the Gap outcomes since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Parliament has discussed Closing the Gap outcomes through motions, ministerial statements, and committee estimates. On 20 March 2025, the House recognised Close the Gap Day and passed a motion acknowledging the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, signed in July 2020, which established 17 socio-economic targets and four priority reforms. The motion also commended the Coalition of Peaks and called on the Government to remain accountable for progress by working in genuine partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisations.

In a question to the Leader of the Government in the NSW Legislative Council, the Hon. John Ruddick raised an Auditor-General's report on the *Governance of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap in NSW*, which found inadequate oversight of $222 million allocated in 2020 and that in about half of cases funding had no tangible outcome. The Hon. Penny Sharpe responded that the Government is working with NSW CAPO to strengthen governance and deliver on the report's recommendations.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, ministers and senators have referenced the Productivity Commission's 2024 review and the government's tabling of the *Closing the Gap 2024 annual report* and *2025 implementation plan*. Senator O'Sullivan asked about the 2024 outcome for target 3, and departmental official Ms Winslow noted the Productivity Commission will report on the current target in July, with a refreshed target 3 expected to include enrolment, attendance and other indicators. Senator Thorpe questioned whether the agreement should be overhauled, stating that targets around incarceration will not be met by 2031 and that outcomes in many areas are getting worse.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Statewide Treaty Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
The Victorian Parliament debated the Statewide Treaty Bill 2025, with Labor and Greens members speaking in support and Liberal and Nationals members opposing it. Supporters described it as a "historic day for Victoria" and a "landmark" that establishes Gellung Warl, a statutory body representing First Peoples, comprising the First Peoples' Assembly, an accountability arm and a truth-telling arm. They argued treaty is about "practical self-determination," giving First Peoples a real say in decisions affecting them, and that it builds on the Yoorrook Justice Commission's truth-telling work. One Labor member said the bill "does not change the Victorian or Commonwealth constitutions," does not establish a third chamber of Parliament, and does not have veto powers, while another stated it is "not about creating a new legal framework but about enhancing the inclusion of First People within the existing systems of law and policy."

Opponents, including the Shadow Minister for Aboriginal Affairs and other Liberal and Nationals members, said they oppose the bill in full and would repeal it within the first 100 days if elected. They argued it "separates Victorians based on race," creates a body "accountable to no-one" with automatic escalating funding starting at $24 million a year and rising beyond $70 million, and undermines parliamentary processes. One member claimed the bill "establishes a vastly different system of law and regulations that separates Victorians based on race," while another said it is "a fourth level of government created for one group of citizens, funded by all and accountable to none." A Scrutiny of Acts and Regulations Committee alert digest was tabled, with one committee member noting the bill's framework "ensures that Gellung Warl operates independently of ministerial direction while maintaining transparency and accountability through annual reports and parliamentary engagement."

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Inquiries Amendment (Yoorrook Justice Commission Records and Other Matters) Bill 2024?
sections.answer:
The Inquiries Amendment (Yoorrook Justice Commission Records and Other Matters) Bill 2024 was debated in the Victorian Parliament, with the Labor government and the Greens supporting it and the Liberals and Nationals opposing it. The bill amends the Inquiries Act 2014 and the Public Records Act 1973 to empower the Yoorrook Justice Commission to make record closure or restriction orders over records of First Peoples' evidence for 99 years after the commission concludes, and to exempt those records from the Freedom of Information Act 1982 for the same period.

Government speakers, including Minister Natalie Hutchins, said the bill responds to recommendations from the Yoorrook Justice Commission and upholds Indigenous data sovereignty principles, giving First Peoples control over access to and use of their evidence. One Labor member said the bill is "trauma informed" and gives a "sense of control" to people who have provided evidence, while another said it is about "listening to our First Nations people" and "closing the gap". The Minister for Treaty and First Peoples said the commission's power to issue record orders only over First Peoples' evidence is a "special measure" that does not constitute discrimination, given First Peoples' unique experiences of trauma and intergenerational trauma.

Opposition speakers argued the bill creates "two classes of citizen" based on race and is "divisive". The Shadow Minister for Aboriginal Affairs said it "undermines legal equity" and is "legally unnecessary" because existing laws under the Public Records Act 1973 and the Freedom of Information Act 1982 already protect sensitive information. Another Liberal member said the bill "would seek to shut down transparency and integrity" and that "truth should be available to all Victorians, not locked away for 99 years". A Nationals member said the coalition opposes the bill because it "divides the community". The Greens supported the bill but criticised the government for accepting less than 15 per cent of the Yoorrook Justice Commission's recommendations, saying Labor is "cherrypicking the ones that seem politically easy".

sections.question: What has parliament said about Treaty and First Nations?
sections.answer:
Victorian parliamentarians have spoken extensively about treaty with First Peoples, with the Victorian Parliament passing Australia's first treaty legislation. One member described it as "a momentous and emotional moment," noting the Allan government's role in acknowledging "the 65,000 years of history and the experiences of First Peoples." Another said the bill recognises "that First Peoples are not only stakeholders; they are sovereign peoples with the right to shape the systems that affect their lives." A Greens member called treaty "a remarkable and generous gift," while another stated that "Victoria now joins" countries like New Zealand, Canada and the United States "in acknowledging that justice begins with truth, and progress begins with partnerships."

The Greens have strongly supported the treaty framework, with one member welcoming a related motion as "implementing a commitment that was made as part of the treaty act." They argued it would improve accountability by requiring bills to "consider treaty and also explain whether it is or is not consistent with treaty," potentially causing a "moment of pause" before legislation is introduced. Another Greens member thanked the Yoorrook Justice Commission and the First Peoples' Assembly, describing the Treaty Authority as "Victoria's independent umpire" for negotiations.

The Liberal and Nationals opposition opposed the Statewide Treaty Bill 2025, with one member stating they "will not be supporting this legislation" and would repeal it if elected. They raised concerns about the proposed body Gellung Warl operating "independently of ministerial direction," receiving "ongoing taxpayer funding," and being granted "significant exemptions from the Freedom of Information Act." The member also cited a Kurnai elder's letter objecting that the name "Gellung Warl" was "selected without the informed consent of Kurnai Elders," calling it "a serious breach of cultural protocol." They argued the bill lacked a mandate, referencing the 2023 Voice referendum result, and claimed treaty "elevates Indigenous Victorians above their fellow citizens."

Other speakers addressed treaty in the context of broader debates. One Labor-aligned member rejected claims the Victorian process was secret, noting it had been "an open process for the last 10 years" and that the government had "won three elections with this commitment." A federal minister, responding to a question, said the government "will always listen to First Nations people" after the Voice referendum defeat. Several speakers linked treaty to calls for justice, with one saying "we must continue to stand with First Nations communities calling for truth, treaty and justice," and another criticising the government for enacting treaty while simultaneously introducing "adult time for violent crime" laws that would disproportionately affect First Nations people.

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on First Nations between 1993 and 2009?
eras.answer:
A recurring and often adversarial debate over Indigenous affairs between 1993 and 2009, with speakers from both sides of politics trading accusations. One government-aligned speaker, defending the Howard government, claimed that Labor had been in power for 13 years and left "the problems of the Australian Aboriginal community" bigger than ever, while asserting that the government had allocated "the highest level of funding in real terms that we have seen in Australia's history," including $2.3 billion. The same speaker characterised Labor's approach as "divisive politics" and "political rhetoric," and quoted a journalist arguing the government should be judged on whether its policies "manage to improve the lives of indigenous Australians." In contrast, a Labor senator criticised government attitudes as supporting "assimilation as the only way forward" and "paternalism as an adequate attitude," which he said was "clearly counter to the human rights of anybody."

On native title specifically, a government member speaking on the Native Title Amendment Bill 2009 said he supported the bill in principle but was deeply critical of the 1993 Native Title Act's effects. He claimed that in his 2.3 million square kilometre electorate he had "never seen anything good" come from native title determinations, alleging that cash flows and royalties had "created death or at least long-term ill health" and that determinations about claimant groups were "creating mayhem in communities." A Labor senator, by contrast, praised the original 1993 Act's negotiation process, noting that "Indigenous leaders were actively involved in the negotiations surrounding its introduction," which contributed to the finding that its measures were special measures. The same senator also paid tribute to David Ross and Peter Yu, former chairs of the Indigenous Land Corporation, describing them as "two great indigenous Australians" who had been "at the forefront of defending indigenous people" during the Wik amendments debate.

On the United Nations Draft Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, an Australian Democrats senator urged the government to adopt it, arguing that indigenous peoples have "the right to maintain and strengthen their distinct political, legal, economic, social and cultural institutions." A government senator responded that Australia had been "intimately and constructively involved" in the declaration's development over more than a decade, and cautioned against rushing its consideration. The record also includes a 2008 apology debate, with one speaker calling the apology "a very important acknowledgement and acceptance of previous actions" and a step towards "a collective better future," while another noted that the rate of Aboriginal children being removed by welfare authorities had "actually increased" since the old policies ended about 25 years earlier.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on First Nations between 2010 and 2019?
eras.answer:
Between 2010 and 2019, policy and public debate on First Nations issues centred on constitutional recognition, the proposed Indigenous voice to parliament, and the Closing the Gap framework. In 2010, the Gillard government "established a process of working towards amending our Constitution to remove racist provisions and to fully recognise and acknowledge our relationship and the relationship that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians have with this nation," appointing an expert panel in December 2010. A Labor speaker noted that "change can only happen when there is majority support for any referendum put to the people" and that the level of support needed "is not yet there." By 2018, the Joint Select Committee on Constitutional Recognition Relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples had travelled across Australia, held 27 hearings, and received nearly 500 submissions; its final report "endorses the proposal for a voice" and recommends a co-design process between government and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

The Uluru Statement from the Heart was a recurring point of contention. A Labor speaker said the statement "was promptly rejected out of hand by this government," while another Labor MP described the rejection as "bitterly disappointing" and criticised the government for "the scandalous notion that somehow this would be a third chamber to the parliament." Labor speakers repeatedly called for a voice to parliament, a makarrata commission for truth-telling and agreement-making, and an early referendum, arguing that "answers will be found in listening to First Nations people." A government backbencher defended the government's record, citing the Prime Minister's Indigenous Advisory Council, the Prime Minister's annual week in a remote community, and three rounds of consultation in the Northern Territory, while rejecting Greens amendments because "they confuse consultation with a much stronger concept of consent."

On Closing the Gap, a Labor speaker in 2018 said most targets "will not be met," that "the gap widens," and that health expenditure on Indigenous Australians excluding hospitals "is falling when it should be increasing." The same speaker noted that the 2008 National Partnership Agreement on Remote Indigenous Housing was due to deliver 4,000 new houses and 7,500 refurbishments by 2018, but that the 2018 budget contained "no further funding" for it. Another Labor MP, speaking in 2019, said targets were not being met and that in some areas, such as Indigenous female life expectancy, "we're going backwards," citing a 32 per cent increase in the Indigenous suicide rate between 1998 and 2015 and an HTLV-1 crisis "at epidemic proportions" in some remote communities. A government speaker acknowledged that "none of us has had a terrific track record on it despite enormous goodwill on both sides and the billions of dollars which have been invested," and defended government priorities around school attendance, work and community safety, claiming school attendance rates had risen by 15 percentage points in some places and that 5,000 jobs had been created through VTEC.

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on First Nations between 2020 and the middle of 2024?
eras.answer:
Policy and public debate on First Nations between 2020 and mid-2024 centred heavily on the proposed First Nations Voice, both at state and federal levels, alongside ongoing efforts to address disadvantage through measures like Closing the Gap. In South Australia, the First Nations Voice Bill 2023 was debated extensively. Supporters, including a Labor member who spoke of being raised on Nukunu land, framed it as a historic step to "change the way we as a parliament and government engage with Aboriginal people here in South Australia from now and for generations to come," and as a state-based version of the Uluru Statement from the Heart. They argued it would help prevent "atrocious laws and policies" of the past and give First Nations people "a seat at the table." Opponents, including several Liberal members, argued the bill would not deliver practical outcomes. One member said it "creates its own layers of bureaucracy" and expressed fear it "will fall short of delivering on some of the key injustices and inequality faced by Indigenous communities," citing disparities in education, incarceration, health, life expectancy and income. Another called it "poor legislation that will not deliver real, positive outcomes for my community," while a third said it was "not about outcomes; it is about adding another layer of government, another layer of bureaucracy" and raised concerns about cost, consultation and constitutional change.

The federal debate also featured prominently. One senator urged support for the upcoming referendum on a federal Voice, calling it "such an important moment for our nation," while another said the debate was "past time having" because the Uluru Statement had "sat on the last government's desk" for five years. A government member described the referendum as "a truly transformational moment for First Nations and real, lasting change: recognition in the Constitution and ability to make representation." In Victoria, the Children and Health Legislation Amendment (Statement of Recognition, Aboriginal Self-determination and Other Matters) Bill 2023 was supported by a Nationals member who said it was "an incremental step in improving the system for Indigenous youth and families," noting the state's failure to reduce over-representation of Aboriginal children in care. In New South Wales, the government reported that findings from its 2023–24 Indigenous Expenditure Report would be used by First Nations communities and organisations "in partnership with government to consider and design appropriate policy responses," and that First Nations Impact Assessments were piloted as part of the 2024–25 budget process.

The record also shows specific budget allocations and expenditure. In 2023–24, the largest shares of First Nations-specific expenditure were budgeted for housing and community amenities ($301.8 million), education ($237.8 million) and social protection ($226.3 million). A 2020 Senate motion on COVID-19 and First Nations was defeated 29–30, with Labor, Greens and crossbench senators voting in favour and Coalition senators, Pauline Hanson and others against. One senator criticised government policy as still "literally killing First Nations peoples" despite repeated reports, while another acknowledged that "we are very far from an antiracist Australia" and that "First Nations people continue to face the worst kinds of discrimination." A government member also noted that First Nations knowledge and leadership "will play an important role in our nation's response to climate change."

key_moments.title: Northern Territory Emergency Response Bills
key_moments.speaker: Nigel Scullion
key_moments.brief: The Minister for Families, Community Services and Indigenous Affairs, Mal Brough, tabled the Australian Government's response to a committee inquiry into welfare payment reform bills for the Northern Territory emergency response, agreeing in full to five recommendations and in part to two, and stating that compensation would be paid under the Constitution and that the bills were drafted as special measures under the Racial Discrimination Act.
key_moments.why: Northern Territory Emergency Response Bills, Federal, 2007

key_moments.title: Stolen Generation Compensation Bill 2008
key_moments.speaker: Andrew Bartlett
key_moments.brief: The speaker reintroduced a bill to provide monetary compensation to Stolen Generations victims, modelled on Tasmania’s scheme which distributed $5 million among 106 applicants, and criticised the federal government for rejecting compensation while supporting the national apology.
key_moments.why: Second reading, Stolen Generation Compensation Bill 2008, 2008

key_moments.title: Native Title Amendment (Reform) Bill 2011
key_moments.speaker: Rachel Siewert
key_moments.brief: The Native Title Amendment (Reform) Bill 2011 was introduced to address the failure of the Native Title Act to deliver meaningful rights, proposing amendments including a rebuttable presumption of continuity, strengthened good faith negotiation requirements, allowing profit sharing in arbitration, and implementing principles from the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
key_moments.why: Second reading, Native Title Amendment (Reform) Bill 2011, 2011

key_moments.title: Constitutional recognition and the Uluru Statement
key_moments.speaker: Linda Burney
key_moments.brief: The 1967 referendum, which achieved a 90.77% yes vote nationally, is being commemorated alongside the 25th anniversary of the High Court's Mabo decision; the speaker also noted upcoming discussions for a proposed referendum to recognise Aboriginal people in the Australian Constitution, drawing on the Uluru Statement, Patrick Dodson’s expert panel, and a parliamentary committee’s work.
key_moments.why: Constitutional recognition and the Uluru Statement, Federal, 2017

key_moments.title: Closing the Gap statement
key_moments.speaker: Sharon Claydon
key_moments.brief: Progress on Closing the Gap is mixed: child mortality, early childhood education and Year 12 attainment are on track, but literacy, numeracy, employment, life expectancy and school attendance are failing. The speaker argued that failures stem from a lack of genuine partnership with Indigenous communities and community-owned programs, and supported Labor’s initiatives including the Uluru Statement from the Heart, additional targets on incarceration and out-of-home care, and compensation for the stolen generations.

key_moments.title: Summary Offences Amendment (Decriminalisation of Public Drunkenness) Bill 2020 - Second reading
key_moments.speaker: Tim Read
key_moments.brief: The speaker supported the decriminalisation of public drunkenness bill but criticised the Andrews government for the disproportionate rise in Aboriginal incarceration from 12 to 16 times the rate of non-Indigenous Victorians under its policies. They named Tanya Day’s family, campaigners Belinda Stevens, Apryl Watson, Warren Stevens and Kimberly Watson, and cited 434 Aboriginal deaths in custody since the 1991 royal commission recommendation.
key_moments.why: Second reading, Summary Offences Amendment (Decriminalisation of Public Drunkenness) Bill 2020, 2021

key_moments.title: First Nations Voice Bill
key_moments.speaker: Nat Cook
key_moments.brief: The speaker argued that parliament should pass the First Nations Voice Bill 2023, calling it a historic moment to deliver on the Uluru Statement from the Heart and address systemic disadvantage faced by Aboriginal people. They highlighted the Labor government's extensive consultation with Aboriginal communities, criticised the Liberal opposition's claims of a rushed process, and urged all members to support the bill.
key_moments.why: First Nations Voice Bill, South Australia, 2023
